Date: 2025-11-18
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 1:07
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Rory Patel (Redwood Product), Dana Rivera (Catalyst Head of ML), Samir Gupta (Catalyst Platform), Priya Menon (Catalyst Security), Oliver Park (Catalyst PM)
summary: Redwood ran a migration/demo session focused on how Catalyst AI can map their OpenAI/Anthropic/Together usage to Redwood API equivalents. Covered model parity mapping, function calling differences, streaming and token accounting, embeddings migration, and Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching/caching/quantization to lower unit cost. Security questions (SOC2, KMS, VPC/private deployments) were raised; next steps are a short dedicated pilot, parabity spreadsheet, and security docs share.
topics: Agenda: 1) Quick intake & constraints, 2) parity mapping (models + params), 3) live console/API walkthrough, 4) Optimize cost levers, 5) security & deployment patterns, 6) next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyoone, thanks for joining — we're gonna run through a migration demo today, show how we map the stuff you currently run on OpenAI/Anthropic/Together over to Redwood, quick cost parity, and some perf/ops knobs.
[00:12] Dana Rivera: Thanks — excited — we have limited time — we mostly want to know: how close is the output behavior, how much lift to change API calls, and what the cost delta looks like.
[00:22] Liam O'Neill: Cool. I'll kick off with a high-level parity map and then do a quick live API call from the console. Note in this session we'll use imperfect transcriptions so sorry in advance for any name mixups.
[00:33] Samir Gupta: Also, our stack: currently prod calls go to OpenAI (gpt-4o for chat, ada-ish for embeddings) and we have a small Anthrapic account for safety experiments — apologies, anthrapic — Anthropic — and some Together models for cheaper ops. We're on K8s, some calls route via our API gateway, and we need SSO + VPC for dedicated.
[00:48] Liam O'Neill: Good context. First: model parity. On the mapping sheet (we'll share), gpt-4o maps to rdx-4o; gpt-4o-mini -> rdx-4o-lite; Claude-2 -> rdx-c2-compatible (same tokenization but slightly different system prompt behavior). Together's mix of small models we map to rdx-3-quant or rdx-3-ls depending on sequence length.
[01:12] Dana Rivera: When you say "map", how much do we need to tweak prompts? We depend on system prompts and function calling heavily.
[01:20] Liam O'Neill: Two parts. Syntactic parity is easy: our API supports the same chat/message envelope, function calling (we map parameters to Redwood's call structure), and streaming. Semantic parity — exact output — needs light prompt tuning; often changing the system prompt by 1-2 lines or adding a few examples gets within A/B parity. We'll provide a suggested set of prompt deltas in the spreadsheet.
[01:45] Rory Patel: To add, our function-calling implements the same 'name/arguments' contract. The main difference is our error semantics for partial parses — Redwood returns a structured failure reason and automatic fallback to raw text generation which you can toggle in the console.
[01:58] [02:00] Liam O'Neill: Now a quick live call. I'm going to run a simple chat call using the console. (typing, UI clicks audible)
[02:12] Speaker 2: [background] — there's a tiny lag, but looks fine.
[02:18] Liam O'Neill: The call GOES out, streamed tokens start at 02:22. Redwoods stream frames are chunked a bit differently — you get thinner frames but more frequent ones which helps low-latency clients.
[02:30] [02:30] Dana Rivera: How does token accounting compare? Our billing ties to tokens from OpenAI, we use tokenizers across the pipeline.
[02:38] Liam O'Neill: Great question. Redwood uses the same byte-pair tokenization family for common models, but token counts can differ by a few percent. We include a token-translation table in the parity sheet. For cost modeling we give you tokens-per-prompt and tokens-per-response estimates using your sample prompt set.
[02:55] Samir Gupta: Do you support streaming function call events or do we have to buffer? We rely on partial outputs.
[03:02] Liam O'Neill: We stream function call events. There's a 'partialArgs' frame in our stream that's similar to the partial-args/delta frames used by other providers.
